To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a change in the resuscitation protocol in Tucson (USA) has been instituted based upon historical database information; 2) a randomized trial is not feasible to test this change; 3) an externally controlled trial has been instituted to test the effectiveness of this change; and 4) this externally controlled trial is the first of its kind to be conducted in the United States of America.

the Tucson Fire Department has been using an externally controlled clinical trial approach to advance resuscitation science and has made significant improvements in survival from out-of-hospital ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest.

the Tucson Fire Department has a poor bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) rate, a lack or response to initial defibillation after prolonged ventricle fibrillation (VF) and substantial time without CPR during the resuscitative effort.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new resuscitation protocols and their implementation in a community.
improving resuscitation science and survival from cardiac arrest.
the development of a resuscitation protocol based upon an alternative approach to advancing our science, one that uses historical data to guide protocol changes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a formalized evidence-based approach to the formulation of resuscitation guidelines is the optimal method.
externally controlled clinical trials should be given more consideration in the development of resuscitation guidelines.
externally controlled clinical trials are an acceptable source of evidence to be included in ILCOR Guideline formulation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the resuscitation process is complex, and that there is a need for a more comprehensive, multifaceted approach to advancing resucidation science.
we have used a database to identify resuscitation issues, and have instituted protocol changes based upon the information.

the Tucson Fire Department, in conjunction with local emergency medical services and hospital emergency departments, is attempting to change our resuscitation protocols based upon a review of the historical database.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a local database can provide valuable information that is not available in the published literature.

local data can be very useful in formulating resuscitation protocols and in changing resuscitation practice, and that such changes should not necessarily await the results of randomized controlled clinical trials.
a formalized evidence-based approach to resuscitation science may be too cumbersome to allow rapid change of resuscitation protocols.
